mainTopic: Shared damages with a disqualified sacred ox, רבא's rules for an ox and a person pushing into a pit, and the exemption for vessels in a pit
overview: The amud opens with an ordinary ox and a blemished בכור that gore together. The בכור can never be redeemed, so its owner pays nothing, and אביי and רבינא argue about how much the owner of the ordinary ox pays. The גמרא explains their argument through רבנן and רבי נתן, or through the difference between a תם ox and a מועד ox, and it also brings a second version of their argument. Next, רבא teaches that when an ox and a person push something into a pit, each damager pays only the kinds of payment the תורה puts on it. He also rules that the pit owner is exempt for a disqualified sacred animal, learning this from 'והמת יהיה לו.' The גמרא asks how רבא could state this plainly when he once raised it as a question, and answers that he later resolved it. It then explains why the pit verse teaches this exemption while the matching ox verse teaches that the owner keeps the carcass. Finally, the גמרא turns to the משנה's rule that a pit owner is exempt for broken vessels. It shows that רבי יהודה disagrees and starts to ask how the רבנן explain the word 'or' in the פסוק, a question that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The case: an ordinary ox and a disqualified sacred ox gore together
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא presents a case of two oxen goring together, one ordinary and one a disqualified קָדָשִׁים animal, and asks what kind of animal that second ox is.
steps.simpleTranslation: An ordinary ox and a disqualified sacred ox that gored together: what is this second ox?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new case and immediately asks what exactly is meant by a 'disqualified sacred ox.' It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most disqualified קָדָשִׁים can be redeemed and become ordinary animals that belong to a person. The גמרא needs a case where the sacred ox stays sacred, so it asks which animal is meant.

keyTerms.meaning: Sacred animals that became unfit for the altar, usually because of a blemish
They gored
What is it? (a request to define the case)

phrases.english: An ox and a disqualified consecrated ox that gored together
What is this case?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which kind of disqualified sacred ox is being discussed?

steps.title: It is a firstborn ox that cannot be redeemed
steps.stepSummary: The disqualified sacred ox is a בכור, which can never be redeemed even after it gets a blemish.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a firstborn ox, which one does not redeem.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the case is a blemished בכור. A בכור is never redeemed, so it keeps its sacred status.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the בכור is never redeemed, it is never treated as an ordinary privately owned ox. So its owner does not pay for its damage, and the whole question becomes how much the owner of the ordinary ox pays.

keyTerms.meaning: A firstborn male animal, holy from birth and given to a כהן
Redeems (exchanges sacred status for money)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the בכור stops being holy once it is blemished. It can be eaten by a כהן, but it is never redeemed, and that is the whole point here.

phrases.english: A firstborn ox,
which one does not redeem;
phrases.notes: It became blemished and unfit for the altar, but a בכור can never be redeemed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It is a blemished בכור, which cannot be redeemed.

steps.title: אביי says half the damage, רבינא says a quarter
steps.stepSummary: אביי rules that the owner of the ordinary ox pays half the damage, and רבינא rules he pays only a quarter.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: he pays half the damage. רבינא said: he pays a quarter of the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים argue about how much the owner of the ordinary ox must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner of the בכור pays nothing, so the only question is the ordinary ox's share. אביי says half, and רבינא says only a quarter. The next steps explain where each number comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: Half the damage
A quarter of the damage
Pays

phrases.english: Abaye says: He pays half the damage,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the owner of the regular ox.

phrases.english: Ravina says: He pays a quarter of the damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling on the case just defined.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי: the ordinary ox's owner pays half the damage. רבינא: he pays a quarter.

steps.title: First explanation: both speak of a תם ox, following רבנן or רבי נתן
steps.stepSummary: Both are talking about a תם ox. רבינא follows רבנן (each damager is responsible for half), and אביי follows רבי נתן (each damager can be held for everything).
steps.simpleTranslation: Both are talking about a תם ox. This one follows the רבנן, and that one follows רבי נתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the argument: they agree the ox is a תם, but they follow two different opinions about two damagers who acted together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבנן, the ordinary ox is responsible for only its half, and a תם pays half of that, which is a quarter (רבינא). According to רבי נתן, it is responsible for the whole damage when the other side cannot pay, and a תם pays half of that, which is half (אביי).

keyTerms.meaning: An ox without a history of goring; it pays only half the damage
The Sages, who hold that each partner in damage pays his own share

steps.confusionAlert: The order is reversed. 'הא כרבנן' goes with רבינא (the quarter), and 'והא כרבי נתן' goes with אביי (the half).

phrases.english: Both this and that are about an innocuous ox;
this one follows the Rabbis,
phrases.notes: This is רבינא: half of his half share equals a quarter.

phrases.english: and that one follows Rabbi Natan.
phrases.notes: This is אביי: half of the full damage equals half.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the basis of the argument in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the basis for half against a quarter?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Both speak of a תם; רבינא follows רבנן, and אביי follows רבי נתן.

steps.title: Second explanation: both follow רבנן, but תם versus מועד
steps.stepSummary: Alternatively, both follow רבנן. רבינא speaks of a תם ox (quarter), and אביי speaks of a מועד ox (half).
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: both follow the רבנן. This one is about a תם ox, and that one is about a מועד ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a different way to explain the two numbers, so that they do not really argue at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רבנן, the ordinary ox is responsible for half. If it is a תם, it pays half of that, a quarter (רבינא). If it is a מועד, it pays its full share, half (אביי). So the two are just talking about different cases.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say (it introduces another explanation)
An ox with a goring history that has been warned; it pays full damage

steps.whatToRemember: The quarter-versus-half split can come either from רבנן against רבי נתן (both תם), or from תם against מועד (both רבנן).

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
both this and that follow the Rabbis;
this one is about an innocuous ox, that one is about a forewarned ox.
phrases.notes: The תם case is רבינא's quarter; the מועד case is אביי's half.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an alternative to the explanation in step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Both follow רבנן; רבינא speaks of a תם, and אביי of a מועד.

steps.title: Another version: half the damage against full damage
steps.stepSummary: Some report the argument differently: אביי says half, and רבינא says the full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: אביי said half the damage; רבינא said the full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of what אביי and רבינא said. The next step explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, אביי still says half, but רבינא now says the ordinary ox's owner pays everything. The argument now runs between half and full, not between quarter and half.

keyTerms.meaning: The full damage

phrases.english: There are those who say:
Abaye says: half the damage,
Ravina says: the full damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the version of the argument given in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי: half the damage. רבינא: full damage.

steps.title: Explaining the second version: both מועד, רבנן against רבי נתן
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, both speak of a מועד ox. אביי follows רבנן (pays his half share), and רבינא follows רבי נתן (pays everything).
steps.simpleTranslation: Both are about a מועד ox. This one follows the רבנן, and that one follows רבי נתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second version: the ox is a מועד, and the argument is רבנן against רבי נתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מועד pays fully for whatever it is responsible for. Under רבנן, that is its half share, so it pays half (אביי). Under רבי נתן, it covers what the exempt בכור's owner does not pay, so it pays everything (רבינא).
steps.whatToRemember: In the second version, the ox is a מועד: אביי (half) follows רבנן, and רבינא (full) follows רבי נתן.
steps.confusionAlert: Here the order is not reversed: 'הא כרבנן' is אביי, and 'והא כרבי נתן' is רבינא.

phrases.english: Both this and that are about a forewarned ox;
this one follows the Rabbis,
phrases.notes: This is אביי: a מועד pays its full half share.

phrases.english: and that one follows Rabbi Natan.
phrases.notes: This is רבינא: the ordinary ox's owner covers the whole damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the basis of the second version in step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Both speak of a מועד; אביי follows רבנן, and רבינא follows רבי נתן.

steps.title: Both follow רבי נתן, but one speaks of a forewarned ox and one of an ordinary ox
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, where רבינא says full and אביי says half, both can follow רבי נתן. רבינא means a מועד ox, which pays full. אביי means a תם ox, which pays only half.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: both of them follow רבי נתן. This one is talking about a forewarned ox, and that one is talking about an ordinary ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another way to explain the second version of the argument (half against full). Now both אמוראים agree on the principle and simply describe different oxen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי נתן, the ox owner can be made to pay the most an ox owner ever pays. For a מועד ox that is the full damage, so רבינא says full. A תם ox never pays more than half, so אביי says half.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say: an introduction to another possible explanation
This one and that one: both opinions
A forewarned ox with a history of goring, whose owner pays full damage
An ordinary ox with no goring record, whose owner pays half damage

steps.whatToRemember: The second version of the argument can be explained two ways. Either they argue over רבנן against רבי נתן (Step 7), or both follow רבי נתן and they speak of a מועד ox against a תם ox.

phrases.english: If you want, say:
this one and that one both follow רבי נתן;
this one is about a forewarned ox, and that one is about an ordinary ox.
phrases.notes: 'This one' is רבינא, who says full payment. 'That one' is אביי, who says half.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא כְּרַבִּי נָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second explanation of the version in Step 6, alongside the explanation in Step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Both follow רבי נתן. רבינא (full) speaks of a מועד ox, and אביי (half) speaks of a תם ox.

steps.title: רבא sorts out which damager pays for each type of payment
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that when an ox and a person push something into a pit, all three damagers share regular damages. Each other kind of payment, though, applies only to some of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If an ox and a person pushed something into a pit, then for regular damages, all of them are liable. For the four extra payments and for payment for unborn babies, the person is liable, and the ox and the pit are exempt. For ransom and the thirty shekels for a slave, the ox is liable, and the person and the pit are exempt. For vessels and for a disqualified consecrated ox, the person and the ox are liable, and the pit is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא starts a new teaching. He looks at a case with three damagers working together and lists who pays for which kind of loss.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה gives each kind of damager its own set of payments. When several damagers cause one loss together, each one pays only for the kinds of payment the תורה placed on that kind of damager. So each kind of loss can have a different group of payers.

keyTerms.meaning: The four extra payments a person who injures pays: pain, medical costs, lost work, and embarrassment
Payment for unborn babies lost in a miscarriage
Ransom payment owed when a מועד ox kills a person
The thirty shekels owed when an ox kills a slave
Consecrated animals that became blemished and unfit for the altar

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the lists. Regular damages are the only category where all three pay. Each of the other categories leaves out at least one damager.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that shared damage does not mean shared liability for everything. Each damager is judged by its own category in the תורה.

phrases.english: רבא said:
An ox and a person that pushed something into a pit,
regarding damages, all of them are liable.
phrases.notes: 'All of them' means the person, the ox's owner, and the pit's owner.

phrases.english: Regarding the four things
and payment for unborn babies,
the person is liable, and the ox and the pit are exempt.
Regarding ransom and the thirty shekels of a slave,
the ox is liable, and the person and the pit are exempt.
Regarding vessels and an ox that is a disqualified consecrated animal,
the person and the ox are liable, and the pit is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: שׁוֹר וְאָדָם שֶׁדָּחֲפוּ לְבוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching that moves on from the אביי and רבינא argument to a three-damager case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All three pay regular damages. Only the person pays the four extra payments and payment for unborn babies. Only the ox pays ransom and the thirty shekels for a slave. The person and the ox, but not the pit, pay for vessels and for a disqualified consecrated ox.

steps.title: Why is the pit exempt for a disqualified consecrated ox?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of the pit owner's exemption.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: This short question sets up the next step. רבא, continuing his teaching, asks for the source for the pit owner being exempt when a disqualified consecrated ox falls in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question focuses on the last item in רבא's list. The ox and the person pay for this animal, so why does the pit owner go free?

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He is asking why the pit is exempt for the disqualified consecrated ox.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind the last ruling in רבא's list.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that exempts the pit owner for a disqualified consecrated ox.

steps.title: The verse 'and the dead animal shall be his' exempts the pit
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק about a pit says 'the dead animal shall be his.' The pit owner pays only when the dead animal belongs to its owner, so a disqualified consecrated animal is left out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'And the dead animal shall be his.' This means the pit owner pays only for an animal whose carcass belongs to its owner. That leaves out this animal, whose carcass is not his.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers with a פסוק from the section about pits. That פסוק limits when a pit owner has to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the פסוק is written about a pit, it limits only the pit owner's liability. For a disqualified consecrated animal, the dead body does not count as 'his.' So the pit owner is exempt, while the ox and the person still pay.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And the dead animal shall be his' (שמות 21:34)
Leaves out: this case is excluded from the rule

steps.whatToRemember: The pit owner pays only when the dead animal 'belongs to him.' That is why he is exempt for a disqualified consecrated animal.

phrases.english: The verse says:
'And the dead animal shall be his.'
phrases.notes: שמות 21:34

phrases.english: This applies to one whose dead animal is his,
which leaves out this case, where the dead animal is not his.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 10 with a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The words 'the dead animal shall be his' limit a pit owner's liability to animals whose carcass belongs to their owner. A disqualified consecrated animal is therefore excluded.

steps.title: Was this really obvious to רבא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא's clear ruling, since רבא himself once asked this exact question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean רבא found it obvious? But רבא asked it as a question! He asked: if a disqualified consecrated ox falls into a pit, what is the law? Do the words 'and the dead animal shall be his' mean the pit owner pays only when the dead animal belongs to its owner, which leaves out this case? Or do these words come to teach that the owners keep and deal with the carcass?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction. In Step 9 רבא stated the exemption plainly, but elsewhere he asked about it as an open question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 11 the exemption came from reading 'והמת יהיה לו' as 'only when the dead animal is his.' But רבא's own question offers a second reading: the words teach that בעלים מטפלין בנבילה, meaning the owner keeps the carcass. If the words might mean that, the exemption is no longer obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this to say that…? (opens a challenge from a conclusion)
The owners deal with the carcass: it stays theirs, and its value counts toward the payment
Or perhaps

steps.confusionAlert: Both readings explain the same three Hebrew words. The question is which lesson those words teach, not what the words say.

phrases.english: Is this to say that it was obvious to Rava?
phrases.notes: This refers to רבא's ruling in Step 9, that the pit owner is exempt for a disqualified consecrated ox.

phrases.english: But Rava actually raised it as a question!
For Rava asked:
A disqualified consecrated ox
that fell into a pit, what is the law?
Does this 'and the dead animal shall be his'
phrases.notes: שמות 21:34

phrases.english: apply only to one whose dead animal is his,
leaving out this case, where the dead animal is not his?
phrases.notes: The owner of a disqualified consecrated animal may not benefit from its carcass, so in a sense it isn't 'his.'

phrases.english: Or perhaps 'and the dead animal shall be his'
comes to teach that the owners deal with the carcass?
phrases.notes: The carcass stays with the owner, and the damager pays only for the lost value.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דִּפְשִׁיטָא לֵיהּ לְרָבָא? וְהָא מִיבַּעְיָא בָּעֵי לֵיהּ לְרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the derivation given in Step 11 by citing רבא's own doubt about it.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's confident ruling that the pit owner is exempt for a פסולי המוקדשין ox
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא himself treated the verse as open to two readings, so he cannot treat the exemption as obvious.

steps.title: רבא asked, then answered his own question
steps.stepSummary: רבא first asked the question and later resolved it in favor of the exemption.
steps.simpleTranslation: After he asked it, he then resolved it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction. רבא asked the question first, and later decided that the words mean 'only when the dead animal is his.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no real contradiction, because the two statements come from different stages. The question came first, and the clear ruling in Step 9 came after he resolved it.

keyTerms.meaning: After he asked it
He then resolved it

phrases.english: After he asked it,
he then resolved it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different stages: question first, ruling after
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's question shows he never settled the matter.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא settled it in favor of 'only when the dead animal is his,' so the exemption stands.

steps.title: Where does רבא learn that the owner keeps the carcass?
steps.stepSummary: If the pit verse teaches the exemption, where does רבא learn בעלים מטפלין בנבילה?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, where does he learn that the owners deal with the carcass?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up the next move. If רבא used the pit verse for the exemption, he needs a different source for the other lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule that the owner keeps the carcass is accepted הלכה. Since the pit verse is now 'used up' on the exemption, the גמרא asks where that rule comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: From where does he learn it?

phrases.english: But then, that the owners deal with the carcass:
from where does he learn it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בְּעָלִים מִטַּפְּלִין בִּנְבֵילָה – מְנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from Step 13: once the pit verse teaches the exemption, the other lesson needs a source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for בעלים מטפלין בנבילה according to רבא

steps.title: He learns it from the same words said about an ox
steps.stepSummary: The same words, 'והמת יהיה לו', also appear about an ox, and from there רבא learns that the owner keeps the carcass.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from 'and the dead animal shall be his' that is said about an ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the תורה repeats the same words about an ox goring, and רבא learns the carcass rule from there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two verses with identical words: one about בור and one about שור. רבא uses each verse for a different lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: He derives it
Of the ox (the verse about an ox)

phrases.aramaic: נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מִן ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״ דְּשׁוֹר.
phrases.english: He learns it from 'and the dead animal shall be his' said about an ox.
phrases.notes: שמות 21:36

steps.triggerLanguage: נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מִן ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״ דְּשׁוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ox verse teaches בעלים מטפלין בנבילה.

steps.title: Why not switch the two lessons?
steps.stepSummary: Why give the carcass rule to the ox verse and the exemption to the pit verse, and not the other way around?
steps.simpleTranslation: What makes you say that from the ox verse you learn that owners deal with the carcass, and from the pit verse you learn 'only one whose dead animal is his'? I can reverse it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the split. Nothing has yet shown why each verse got its particular lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two verses have identical words, so either one could teach either lesson. If they were switched, the exemption would apply to a goring ox and not to a pit, which would change the הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: What did you see? (why choose this way)
You derive from it
I will reverse it

phrases.aramaic: מַאי חָזֵית דִּ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״ דְּשׁוֹר –
phrases.english: What makes you say that from 'and the dead animal shall be his' said about an ox
you learn that the owners deal with the carcass,
and from 'and the dead animal shall be his' said about a pit
you learn 'only one whose dead animal is his'?
I can reverse it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the split of lessons between the two verses set up in Steps 11 and 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assignment of the exemption to בור and the carcass rule to שור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verses are identical, so the assignment seems arbitrary and could be reversed.

steps.title: The exemption fits pit, which already exempts vessels
steps.stepSummary: It makes sense to put the exemption in בור, since the תורה already exempts a pit for broken vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense to put the exemption with pit, since the תורה exempts it for vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with logic. בור already has an exemption: it does not pay for vessels that fall in and break. So another exemption fits there best.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the תורה is already lenient with בור, adding one more exemption there is natural. The carcass rule then goes to שור.

keyTerms.meaning: It is reasonable
Since
Vessels; a pit owner is exempt when they break in his pit

phrases.english: It makes sense to put the exemption with pit,
since the Torah exempts it for vessels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'reverse it' challenge of Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Logical fit (סברא): an exemption belongs where the Torah is already lenient
steps.terutzMaskana: בור, already exempt for vessels, is the natural place for the exemption.

steps.title: But ox also has an exemption: half damages
steps.stepSummary: On the contrary, ox also has a leniency, since a תם ox pays only half.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary, put the exemption with ox, since the תורה exempts it from half the damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. Ox also has a built-in leniency, so the same logic could put the exemption there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שור תם pays only חצי נזק, so the תורה is lenient with ox too. If 'already lenient' is the test, ox seems to pass it as well.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary
Half damages, paid by a שור תם

phrases.english: On the contrary, put the exemption with ox,
since the Torah exempts it from half the damage!
phrases.notes: This is the תם ox, an ox not known to gore, which pays only half.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the logic of Step 17 around to favor ox.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reasoning of Step 17 that the exemption belongs with בור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Ox also has an existing leniency (חצי נזק), so the logic does not pick out בור.

steps.title: Ox is never fully exempt
steps.stepSummary: Ox is never exempt from the whole damage, but pit is fully exempt for vessels, so pit is the more lenient case.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, we never find ox exempt from the entire damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the pushback. Ox only loses half, while pit can be fully exempt. So the full exemption for a disqualified consecrated animal fits pit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a disqualified consecrated animal, the exemption is total. Only בור already has total exemptions (vessels), while שור always pays at least half. So the original split stands.

keyTerms.meaning: The entire damage
In any case, at least
We do not find

steps.whatToRemember: The pit verse teaches the exemption for an animal that is not 'his' (פסולי המוקדשין). The ox verse teaches בעלים מטפלין בנבילה. The split holds because only בור has full exemptions, while שור always pays at least half.

phrases.english: In any case, an exemption from the entire damage
we do not find for ox.
phrases.notes: The words 'for ox' are not in the text but are understood. A pit, by contrast, pays nothing for broken vessels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the counter-argument of Step 18 and restores the answer of Step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing kinds of leniency: partial versus total
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ox's half-damage leniency makes it just as fitting for the exemption.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only בור has total exemptions, so the total exemption for פסולי המוקדשין belongs there.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: an ox and its vessels fall into a pit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings back the next line of the משנה: an ox with its vessels fell into a pit and the vessels broke.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: If an ox and its vessels fell into the pit and the vessels broke, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a new line from the משנה so it can discuss it. This line sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the pit owner pays for the animal but is exempt for the broken vessels. The previous steps already relied on this exemption for vessels in a בור, and now the גמרא studies this line directly.

keyTerms.meaning: its vessels, the things the animal was carrying or wearing
they broke
and so on; short for the rest of the quote

phrases.english: If an ox and its vessels fell into it,
phrases.notes: 'It' is the pit from the משנה.

phrases.english: and they broke, etc.
phrases.notes: The rest of the משנה says the pit owner pays for the ox but not for the vessels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the discussion of which verse holds which rule to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A pit owner is liable for an animal that falls in, but exempt for the vessels that break with it.

steps.title: The משנה does not follow רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the משנה's exemption for vessels goes against רבי יהודה, who holds the pit owner pays for vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our משנה is not like רבי יהודה, because a ברייתא teaches: רבי יהודה makes a person pay for damage to vessels in a pit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notes who the משנה agrees with. It brings a ברייתא showing that רבי יהודה disagrees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says vessels in a pit are exempt. רבי יהודה says they must be paid for. So the משנה must follow the רבנן, the Sages who argue with רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: our משנה
not in line with רבי יהודה
makes him liable, says he must pay

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the exemption for vessels in a בור is a מחלוקת, not something everyone agrees on.

phrases.english: Our משנה is not in line with רבי יהודה –
as it was taught: רבי יהודה makes one liable
for damage to vessels in a pit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies whose view the newly quoted משנה follows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה follows the רבנן; רבי יהודה holds a pit owner pays for broken vessels.

steps.title: What is the רבנן's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where the רבנן get the exemption for vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the רבנן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source behind the רבנן's view that vessels in a pit are exempt. The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that there are two opinions, the גמרא wants to see each side's reasoning. It starts with the רבנן, whose view the משנה follows.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the reason?
the Sages, the majority who argue with רבי יהודה

phrases.english: What is the reason of the רבנן?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the view the משנה follows.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for exempting vessels in a בור.

steps.title: The פסוק says 'ox or donkey', so not a person and not vessels
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן learn from 'ox' that a person is excluded, and from 'donkey' that vessels are excluded.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the פסוק says: 'And an ox or a donkey falls there.' An ox, and not a person. A donkey, and not vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with the פסוק about a pit. Each animal named in it is read as leaving something out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Naming 'ox' limits liability for death to animals, leaving out a person. Naming 'donkey' limits it to the animal itself, leaving out the vessels it carries. So vessels in a בור are exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: because the פסוק says
and it falls there, into the pit
and not a person

steps.confusionAlert: 'Not a person' means the pit owner does not pay for a person who dies in the pit. It does not mean a pit is never a problem for people.

phrases.english: Because the verse says:
'And an ox or a donkey falls there';
phrases.notes: שמות 21:33

phrases.english: 'Ox' – and not a person,
'Donkey' – and not vessels.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר קְרָא: וְנָפַל שָׁמָּה שּׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the רבנן's source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The words 'ox' and 'donkey' in the פסוק exclude a person and vessels.

steps.title: רבי יהודה reads 'or' as adding vessels
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה uses the extra word 'or' to include vessels in pit liability.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה says the word 'or' comes to include vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי יהודה's reading of the same פסוק. He focuses on the word 'or'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have said 'ox and donkey'. רבי יהודה sees the word 'or' as a hint that adds more cases, and he says it adds vessels. So for him the pit owner pays for vessels.

keyTerms.meaning: or
to include, to add another case

phrases.english: And רבי יהודה – 'or',
comes to include the vessels.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה – אוֹ, לְרַבּוֹת אֶת הַכֵּלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side's reading of the same פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהודה learns from the word 'or' that vessels are included.

steps.title: How do the רבנן explain the word 'or'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to ask what the רבנן do with the word 'or'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן, what do they do with 'or'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to ask how the רבנן explain the word 'or' if they do not use it for vessels. This sets up the next move, which continues past this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually, if a word in a פסוק seems extra, both sides need to explain it. Since the רבנן do not learn vessels from 'or', the גמרא wants to know what they learn from it.

keyTerms.meaning: and the רבנן, how do they deal with this?

phrases.english: And the רבנן –

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns רבי יהודה's use of 'or' into a question for the רבנן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the רבנן learn from the word 'or' in the פסוק.
